grades.quote: switching between different threads more often than necessary will reduce throughput because processor time will be wasted on the overhead of context switching, rather than be available for useful work.
grades.reason: Explains the throughput-cost half: switching threads more often than necessary wastes processor time on context-switch overhead, mainly through reduced cache performance. It doesn't explain how frequent switching improves response time.

grades.quote: Xv6, like many operating systems, allows interrupts and even context switches (via yield) while executing in the kernel. The reason for this is to retain quick response times during complex system calls that run for a long time.
grades.reason: Only briefly says context switches in the kernel retain quick response times, and that interrupts have high CPU overhead. It gives no explanation of the scheduling throughput-versus-responsiveness tradeoff caused by frequent context switches.

grades.quote: Responsiveness:** allowing the computer system to respond quickly to something external to the system, such as a human user or another computer system. Even if one thread is in the midst of a long computation, another thread can respond to the external agent.
grades.reason: Describes why concurrent threads help responsiveness, since another thread can respond while one is busy. It says nothing about context-switch overhead or reduced throughput, so it supplies only the responsiveness background.

grades.quote: Notice that the thread-switching rate is dependent on the overall system load, unlike with a fixed time slice. This means that as a system using CFS becomes more loaded, it will tend to sacrifice some throughput in order to retain a desired level of responsiveness.
grades.reason: Directly describes the tradeoff in CFS: a higher thread-switching rate under load keeps responsiveness at the cost of throughput, and there is a floor on time per thread. It doesn't explain the mechanism of the throughput loss, such as cache or switch overhead.
